newsitem.title: CROATIA: Ruling party holds rally to small crowd in capital.
newsitem.headline: Ruling party holds rally to small crowd in capital.

text.p: Croatia's long- ruling HDZ party drew a smaller crowd than a leading opposition rival at what was meant to be its climactic pre-election rally staged in Zagreb's main square on Friday evening.

Up to 20,000 people turned out to hear President Franjo Tudjman, who heads all HDZ slates for municipal and county elections on Sunday although he is not a candidate, only hours before a 24-hour electoral silence took effect.
Only two years ago, a rally by the nationalist HDZ (Croatian Democratic Union) ahead of parliamentary elections had the same square packed in almost unanimous support.

Friday's crowd filled only about two thirds of the square with space to spare and perhaps half the people could not hear or did not listen closely to Tudjman, 74, an authoritarian former general and only broadly popular politician in Croatia.

Tudjman's HDZ first won general elections in 1990, shortly before Croatia proclaimed independence from federal Yugoslavia. It suffered its first major setback in 1995 when a loose seven-party coalition won a majority in Zagreb.

Tudjman refused to cede power in the capital, exercising a "national security" veto to prevent an opposition takeover. He appointed his own provisional mayor and the affair watered down until the coalition eventually disintegrated.

According to the latest polls, the HDZ looks poised to win most municipalities on Sunday but the outcome in some major cities, including the capital Zagreb, was uncertain. Opposition parties are buoyed by discontent over the economy.

A sign that the times may be changing came on Wednesday when the Social Democrats (SDP), formerly communists, rallied in front of some 40,000 people, staging a show with prominent rock bands obviously aimed at a younger audience.
Another leading opposition rival, the centrist Social Liberals (HSLS), drew about as many people as the HDZ.

The HDZ waged a strong campaign through the state-dominated media meant primarily to discredit other parties as political dilettantes while trumpeting its own role in leading Croatia to independence from Yugoslavia, won in 1991 after a war.
The party relies heavily on the charisma of Tudjman, who is said to be suffering from stomach cancer but has regained vigour and weight of late after extensive treatment.
But his voice on Friday was feeble and strangled. It kept breaking off and never once roared in the furious tone that once characterised him.
"The opposition united upon instructions from abroad to take power in Zagreb and bring about chaos like in Serbia and Albania," Tudjman told the throng.
Western diplomats have dismissed such allegations.

Tudjman's remarks drew mild applause. The crowd interrupted the speech chanting "Franjo, Franjo" a few times, but mainly to drown out a group of soccer fans chanting to protest at Tudjman's renaming of a top Zagreb team a few years ago.
Although the HDZ arranged to have the last in a series of election rallies in Zagreb's sprawling main square, it was one of the smaller crowds Tudjman ever addressed.
A dozen buses were parked behind the square, indicating that a significant number of people were bused from rural HDZ strongholds outside Zagreb to augment the number of spectators.
Heavy security, including special police and anti-sniping units, were deployed on rooftops and among the crowd.
